title: Miso and the Whispering Hollow
markdown:
The house had settled into its sleep-hum: wood, breath, the small noises furniture makes when it thinks no one is counting. Lily lay curled like a question, dreaming, if the moonlight on the coverlet was any clue, of whispers. On her pillow, Miso the rat — toast-coloured whiskers, usually a bundle of errands — was a neat warm ball with a strange feeling in it, not excitement exactly, something more like a tug. Beside him Aurelia, the unicorn from Lily’s favourite book, kept a pale glow even at rest. Her silver mane had opinions about order and had dressed for them in sleep.

Beyond the lane the silver birch woods offered rustle and shadow. Damp earth and jasmine came through the unlatched window. Aurelia felt the pull too, though she translated it into etiquette.

“Honestly, Miso. Manners, even at rest. Slipping out without permission is not done. What if a dewdrop landed crooked in my mane?” She smoothed a strand as if an imaginary breeze had been impolite.

Miso’s nose did a tiny curious wriggle. “Lily is asleep. The moon is a painting. They say Whispering Hollow is haunted.” His tail flicked at the delicious shiver.

Aurelia chimed a scoff. “Nonsense. Shadows and wind. Though it might do for research. One should know the common night-creatures. For contrast.”

A glance like a moonbeam, and they took the forgotten gap Lily had not latched. Cool air greeted them as if it had been waiting with a coat. Pine. Something wilder. The silver birches, under the full moon, stood like pale pillars in a cathedral that had never applied for a licence, leaves rustling secrets they would not submit in writing.

A prickly, determined shape from behind the ferns, like a walking pincushion. “Halt. Who’s there. And at this late hour.” Bartholomew the hedgehog, whose life’s work was other people’s permits, brow in a permanent furrow of suspicion.

“Just us,” Miso chirped, trying for importance, chest puffed to the size of a decision.

“Just us?” Quills stood like a hedge. “Out at night without permission. This needs a permit. Checking for dangers. A plan already approved, detailing expected meetings with supposedly haunted areas, plus protocol for ghostly happenings.”

Aurelia’s sigh barely moved air. “Bartholomew, darling. A short stroll. Night air. Nothing to fear. I am here, after all.” She posed; the horn caught moonlight as if moonlight had requested it.

Bartholomew tutted, pebbles in a tin. “Your presence, while impressive and possibly alarming to moths, is not a substitute for procedure. Step one: identify everyone. Two: state purpose. Three: safe zone. Four: record temperature and dampness. This is all very irregular.”

Miso nudged, urgent. They edged past. Bartholomew, denied a form, began counting daisy petals in case the walkers reappeared before dawn, a full inventory of everything. Deeper: the smell of damp earth and pine needles, comforting if you liked being small in a large place. Moonlight through leaves laid silver and shadow on the floor in a pattern no committee had approved.

Soon a clearing where glow-worms lit the ground like scattered emeralds, pulsing softly. Bartholomew rematerialised, daisy-count and moss-check apparently complete. “This section requires a special way of walking. The glowing plants mean order. Fail, and you may mess up the whole glow-worm population. Natural imbalance. Very serious. I have a note.”

Miso’s curiosity outran the note. He bounced. Aurelia followed with a graceful, faintly annoyed prance. Bartholomew hop-scotched behind, pronouncements echoing. “Left paw forward. No, not that left paw. The other left paw. Keep your balance within the normal limits for walking at night.”

Whispering Hollow sat among ancient oaks whose branches bent like old fingers. A deep quiet hung thicker than mist, the sort that swallows sound and then looks innocent. “Honestly,” Aurelia sniffed, nose wrinkling, “the atmosphere is underdressed. Where are the spooky mists? The ghostly sighs? One expects a haunted place to try a little.”

Miso froze. Tiny ears swivelled. A faint, almost sad rustling that was not the wind: dry leaves sighing. “Listen.”

Before Bartholomew could issue regulations for strange night sounds, or a safety talk on echoes, a new figure stepped from the darkest part of the dark. This unicorn was spectacular in the way fireworks are spectacular: you notice, whether you meant to or not. Her coat was a shimmering cascade of rainbow-coloured light that seemed to come from inside. Her horn was tipped with trapped starlight. Looking at her was nearly a job.

“Ah. I have arrived. The very air hums with my presence, does it not? It always does.” Lumina’s gaze swept Miso, Aurelia, Bartholomew as if they were footnotes. “You must be here for the deep wisdom I bring. This hollow is filled with special feelings. Quite obvious. The faint noises are the wind saying its important thoughts. I, of course, am here to explain them to people like you.” She paused for gasps and clapping that had not been put in the budget.

Aurelia’s eyes rolled toward escape. “Wind with thoughts. I had heard it howled.”

Lumina did not take delivery. “The whispers are the woods, clarified by me. I must leave. Brightness fades among the unpolished.”

Her speech did not calm anything. If anything the whispers grew, braiding into one low sorrowful sound that tugged. They seemed to come from an old signpost leaning nearby, weathered wood etched with marks past reading. Darkness around it thickened into something you could almost put a paw on. Bartholomew’s quills prickled. Miso’s heart drummed. The hollow, for the first time that night, felt truly unsettling: not a game of shadows, a forgotten cry.

Aurelia, for all her pride, felt a shiver that was not about mane-dew. It was for her friends. Polish showed a crack. Bartholomew forgot his carefully made rules; quills shook. Miso, usually the one waiting to be reassured, felt protectiveness rise, larger than his paws, surprising even him. This was no longer a fun haunting. It was sad. Deeply, inconveniently sad.

Then Miso remembered the night’s quiet, the honest step into not-knowing. He took a tiny trembling step toward the post, paws in damp earth. “It does not sound angry,” he squeaked, small and remarkably clear. “It sounds lonely. Like it has been alone a very long time.”

Aurelia saw the step and felt her own resolve arrive without a comb. Rules and polish looked like cobwebs beside a real feeling. “Lonely?” The sharp edge left her voice. She walked to the signpost — not bossy, not hesitant — head low, and spoke past it to the ancient oak, branches bare as pleading arms. “Oh, little oak. You sound very sad. Is there something we can do to help. Is there anything you need.”

Lumina, faced with concern that had not been staged, paused. Her brightness dimmed a shade, as if emotion were a weather she had not packed for. “Lonely? I thought expressive wind. Or perhaps a very dramatic beetle.”

The whispers softened, a century’s held sigh. Then, as if honesty had a doorbell, tiny lights flickered. Fireflies. Hundreds. They circled the signpost and the oak and painted the air gold, not terror, a comforting warmth. The sorrowful sound faded into the insects’ quiet rhythmic hum, a lullaby nobody had commissioned. The thick dark receded.

Bartholomew’s quills found their proper places. He gave a nod so small it might have been a blink. “Well. That certainly was not in the rulebook. But I suppose it worked. Unexpected. Effective.” He muttered about amending the forms in the morning, which, for Bartholomew, was affection.

Aurelia’s smile, when it came, had left vanity in the ferns. She looked at Miso and did not make a speech about bravery. The look was enough. Lumina, for once, was quiet, light gentled by an idea she had not brought with her.

Dawn put rose on the east. They stood until the fireflies finished their shift. The breeze in the leaves had stopped auditioning for a ghost. Miso’s whiskers, toast-coloured, twitched toward home, and Aurelia walked beside him without checking her mane for dewdrops, which, in its way, was the night’s second miracle.
characters: Aurelia (unicorn who worries about appearances), Miso (a toast-coloured rat who takes honest steps)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
